newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambia's Chiluba to appoint new cabinet ministers.
newsitem.headline: Zambia's Chiluba to appoint new cabinet ministers.

text.p: Zambian President Frederick Chiluba has dissolved his cabinet and will appoint a new government from legislators who kept their seats in elections earlier this month, a spokesman said on Thursday.
"The president dissolved his cabinet on Wednesday, November 27," presidential spokesman Richard Sakala told Reuters.
He said there was no word on when the president would name a new team of ministers.

Chiluba and his ruling Movement to Multi-party Democracy (MMD) won a landslide in the November 18 elections. He had been under opposition pressure to scrap his cabinet after the dissolution of parliament a month ahead of the polls.
Law experts had said it was unconstitutional for the cabinet to stay in place after parliament was dissolved, but Chiluba insisted that the constitution allowed his government to remain for 90 days.

Chiluba was sworn in for a second term on November 21 after winning the elections that were boycotted by seven opposition parties, including former president Kenneth Kaunda's United National Independence Party (UNIP).
Kaunda, whose parents were from Malawi, was barred from taking part in the poll by a law excluding candidates with foreign parents.

Chiluba won with over 70 pecent of the vote, but final results from the controversial poll were not yet in 10 days after the ballot, which observers said was marred by a flawed voter registration process and the opposition boycott.

Human Rights Watch Africa criticised the polls in a report released on Thursday, saying the run-up was marked by state intimidation of opposition figures, especially after Kaunda announced a return to active politics in 1995.

"Numerous human rights violations before the November 18 vote seriously undermined the legitimacy of the elections themselves and set a negative tone for the country's development over the next several years," the London-based group said in a report released in Lusaka.

"Human Rights Watch Africa calls on the international community to continue to pressure the government to improve its record on human rights as integral to good governance," it said, adding that countries should continue to hold back financial aid.
Western governments suspended balance of payments support to the impoverished southern African country over the changed constitution that excluded Kaunda from the presidential polls.

Earlier this week Zambian police searched the offices of two election monitoring groups and confiscated documents in what opposition groups said was a government attempt to discourage criticism of the elections.
